We've walked the messy corners thoroughly — that's edge exploration done. Here's everything that's **settled**, in plain terms. Read it as "this is the app we've designed together."

---

### Saving (effortless is the rule)
- Paste a link, and the **title and description fill themselves in** from the page. You review and tweak *before* it's saved.
- Add **labels** as you save — type and they become little pills, with **suggestions from labels you already have** so you never make near-duplicates (and "Recipes" = "recipes", no twins).
- A spot for **your own notes** — your words, separate from the page's blurb.
- Paste a link without the "https://"? Accepted. Paste a sentence? Gently blocked. **The link is the only required thing** — no title needed; you can always save.
- If the page **can't be read**, you're told calmly and can save anyway. If you paste a link **you already have**, it opens the one you've got instead of making a copy (ignoring tracking gunk, but respecting real differences like a different video).

### Finding (the whole point)
- **Browse by label** — pull up "everything filed under recipes."
- **Combine labels**: narrow (both), widen ("either"), or exclude ("not that").
- **Search inside everything** — titles, descriptions, addresses, labels, *and your notes* — with matches highlighted so you see *why* something turned up.
- **Sort** newest / oldest / A–Z.

### Living with your bookmarks
- **Click a card to visit the page** (the everyday thing); a **pencil** edits it (the occasional thing).
- **"To read" pile**: saving puts things on it automatically; opening is just a peek; *you* mark things read when you're done.
- **Set aside** (a drawer — kept but out of the way) vs. **Delete forever** (the trash, guarded).
- **Act on many at once** — select a pile, then mark read, label, set aside, or delete (delete made to pause).
- Cards show a **site icon and a small thumbnail** so the list scans fast, and stay **calm at the extremes** — a gentle welcome when empty, tidy uniform cards even with monster titles or ten labels (nothing actually lost, just trimmed on the card).

### Deliberately **not** in the first version (recorded, not dropped)
- **The app keeping its own copy of each page** so content survives a dead site — you flagged this as the *truest* version of your goal; it's on the record as strongly wanted, to be scoped honestly rather than rushed.
- **Dead-link help** — when you click something that's gone, offer to set it aside or find an archived copy.
- A separate look at that **"either/not" combining** stays available; nothing there is pending.

---

That's **15 settled flows**. Edge cases are explored, the main way you interact is nailed down, and your recent reactions have been refinements rather than new directions.

The scene: it's six months later, you click your saved beans recipe, and **the original site is gone** — a 404. There's a calm red bar saying so, and below it, *your kept copy*. The switch shows the three ways that copy could work. In all three, **your note survives** — that's non‑negotiable and cheap regardless.

- **A — Readable copy:** the recipe's text and main photo, saved clean, your note on top. Light, searchable, survives almost anything. Loses exact layout/interactive bits.
- **B — Full page snapshot:** a picture of the whole page as it looked. Pixel‑exact, but heavy, not searchable, and can't capture login/paywalled pages.
- **C — Archived elsewhere:** not your own copy — a pointer to a public web archive if one exists. Nearly free, but not truly *yours*, and can vanish too.

My honest read, for you to push on:

> For *your* goal — recipes, articles, tools you want the actual words and pictures of — **A (readable copy) is the strongest first pass.** It's the one that's genuinely *yours*, survives the site dying, stays searchable (so it still turns up in your search and notes), and doesn't bloat storage. I'd make **A the core**, always keep your note, and use **C as an automatic fallback** only when a page can't be captured (so you still get *something*). **B (pixel snapshot) I'd hold** for later — it's where the cost and the paywall/login limits bite hardest, and it's the least aligned with "find it again by my words."

Two things to decide, in your terms:

1. **When you picture opening a saved copy of a dead page — which of these is "mine"?** Does the readable copy (A) give you the "phew, it's still here" feeling, or is exact‑look (B) something you'd genuinely miss for the things you save?
2. **This one needs the server piece to exist** — so it's a bigger build than what we've done, and it's the moment the app grows a back end. Are you comfortable with that being the shape of this cycle, or would you rather I first prototype *just the experience* (open‑dead‑page → here's your copy) so you can approve the feel before we commit to the heavier plumbing?

The readable copy (A) is the one that feels like *mine*.** For the stuff I actually save — recipes, articles, how-tos — what I want back is the *content*: the ingredients, the method, the picture. So no — exact-look (B) is not something I'd genuinely miss for my things. Where A really wins me over is that it **stays searchable** — a saved copy I could still find by typing "parmesan rind" or by my own note six months later is enormously more useful to me than a frozen picture I can only stare at. Your "A now, C as an automatic fallback when a page can't be copied, B held for later" reads exactly right to me. I'd add just one thing that's non-negotiable, same as the note: **the copy has to be made quietly and automatically the moment I save**, for everything, in the background — because by the time I click a dead link six months on, it's far too late to start copying. If it only grabs a copy when I remember to ask, I'll never remember, and the one time I need it it won't be there.

On the build — I'm comfortable this is the one that earns a back end.** Everything else we kept light on purpose, but this is the feature I said mattered most, and if keeping my own copies is what needs the heavier plumbing, then it's worth it.
